newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU criticised for delays in treaty talks.
newsitem.headline: EU criticised for delays in treaty talks.

text.p: The pace and scope of the inter-governmental conference (IGC) were sharply criticised on Wednesday for being so modest they threatened prospects for enlargement into eastern Europe.

In a speech to the European Parliament, European Commission President Jacques Santer said EU member states were setting their sights too low in the IGC. He questioned their commitment to move the bloc forward.
"A lack of dynamism, ambitions pitched too low -- those are the impressions given by the discussions at the moment," he said.
The EU had to reform the way it worked before accession negotiations with EU hopefuls such as Poland, Hungary and the Baltic states could begin.

"I am in favour of enlargement," Santer said. "But I must make clear that the scenario will come to nothing if the IGC does not provide a solution to the institutional challenges posed by enlargement."
Santer's blunt presentation reflected growing concern in some EU circles that the IGC talks -- which began in March and are due to end in mid-1997 -- have become bogged down.
The talks are designed to prepare the EU for an influx of new members by changing such things as the way decisions are taken and the representation of countries in EU institutions.
EU leaders are due to meet in a special European Council in Dublin on October 5 to discuss the IGC. But leaders have warned against any expectations from the meeting.
"(It) will not be a decision-making summit," Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, the summit host, told a news conference.
He said his fellow leaders wanted to have an informal discussion, but that they intended to give "a substantial impulse" to the talks.

Bruton, whose country is currently the EU president, told the parliament that contrary to the criticisms, the IGC was progressing well and that things were on track for a draft treaty to be presented as a second Dublin summit in December.
"We are moving from the aspirational to the concrete," he said.
But Bruton also said that unless the IGC reformed the EU's institutions, enlargement plans could come unstuck.
"There cannot be enlargement of the Union unless there is a successful conclusion to the inter-governmental conference," Bruton told a news conference.
Responding to a question, he said that this meant that even countries like Britain, which is reluctant to give up sovereignty but which is keen on enlargement, would have to give ground.
"There is going to be pressure on everybody, including Britain, to rally to a reasonable compromise," he said.
Bruton, who earlier gave a passionate speech on what Europe should be also rounded on MEPs and others whom he said were painting a bleak picture of the state of the Union.
"The European Union is having a problem because of its success," he said.
Earlier MEPs had criticised EU member states for not making the Union more meaningful to its citizens.
"The Union is dismally uninspiring," Socialist MEP leader Pauline Green said.
Santer, meanwhile, sought to dismiss any idea that the current negotiations could be finished by mid-1997 and that important remaining issues could be left to a second IGC.
"The mind boggles at the idea of holding a second IGC, a play-off as it were, before the end of the century," Santer said.
"I must emphatically discourage any such notion. Do we really want to carry on external (membership) negotiations and discussions on internal institutional reform at the same time?" he said.
"Do we really want all that to coincide with extremely difficult discussions on future financial perspectives?" he said.
Touching on the thorny issue of decision-making, Santer said the bloc could not handle an influx of newcomers under current rules.
"Maintaining unanimity would kill the Union. Maintaining the complexity of the decision-making procedures would paralyse it," he said.
